derivable_answer: In AI-generated fiction, 'formal range' specifically means the dispersion and coordination among measured stylistic features (not narrative elements like plot or characterization). 'Overclosure' describes a corpus-level condition where generated texts remain locally fluent and coherent but exhibit an unusually restricted tendency across measured formal dimensions. 'Variance overclosure' means novels differ very little from one another across individual features (such as lexical diversity, entropy, sentence length, readability), whereas 'correlational overclosure' is an exploratory hypothesis that features not mechanically related become more strongly coordinated across texts than in human comparators. They differ because a corpus can be variance-restricted without its variables becoming interdependent, or vice versa.

derivable_answer: Highly edit-robust LLM watermarks create a security vulnerability known as piggyback spoofing, where an adversary alters critical content while the watermark retains attribution. The Cocktail watermarking scheme resolves this by co-embedding two complementary signals into each generated token: a robust signal and a fragile signal that share the same mechanism but use independent keys and different seeding windows over normalized text. At detection, their joint scores form a two-dimensional space supporting three-state detection: Intact, Tampered, and No-Watermark.

derivable_answer: Conventional OWOD frameworks fail in sparsely annotated open environments because they rely on dense annotations; under sparse settings, unlabeled known objects blur the boundary between known and unknown categories. Conventional SAOD frameworks fail because they operate under a closed-world assumption and misinterpret unlabeled objects as background, introducing false-negative supervision. In the DPOD framework, KTRM recovers missing known objects to stabilize pseudo-label learning and enforce known-unknown feature separation, while DDTG discovers additional unknown instances via cross-view semantic disagreement/inconsistency.

derivable_answer: The visual grounding framework combines discriminative grounding with reconstructive regularization by jointly supervising shared visual features during training with two objectives: a discriminative Modulated Attention-Contrastive Head (mACH) and a reconstructive JEPA auxiliary stream. It incurs no inference overhead because the JEPA branch is removed after training. The mACH reformulates query-text interaction into a broadcasted computation topology where visual features are broadcast along the batch dimension, allowing a single visual forward pass to simultaneously interact with an arbitrary number of linguistic expressions.
